title: Petaling Street Food: What to Eat in KL's Chinatown
metaDescription: Petaling Street food in KL's Chinatown: breakfast, asam laksa, Hokkien mee, lala noodles, halal tips and the bus from KLIA2 to Pudu Sentral.

contentBlocks.content: Petaling Street food is the reason most people walk into KL's Chinatown hungry. Tourism Malaysia describes Petaling Street as a wet market that is busy from the early morning and a street market that comes alive in the evening, with a large choice of Chinese food and dim sum (Tourism Malaysia). This guide takes you through what to eat in Petaling Street from breakfast to dinner: kopitiam breakfasts, noodle shops, the hawker stalls and food court, and sit-down places for the evening. It also covers how halal works on a mixed street and how to get here from KLIA2.
Key Takeaways
When is Petaling Street open? Tourism Malaysia lists 8am to 8pm from Sunday to Friday and 8am to 10pm on Saturday (Tourism Malaysia). Individual shops keep their own hours.
What do I eat first? Hokkien mee or chee cheong fun at Kim Lian Kee, lala noodles at Lai Foong, raw fish porridge at Hon Kee, and egg tarts at Bunn Choon (Pelago), (Bunn Choon).

Is Petaling Street food halal? It is mixed. Tourism Malaysia lists both halal and non-halal places in the area, and many of the Chinese stalls are non-halal (Tourism Malaysia). Ask at each stall and look for the JAKIM halal certificate at the counter.
Where do I go for breakfast? Jalan Balai Polis and Jalan Hang Lekir, where the kopitiam, the porridge stall and the dim sum shop sit within a few doors of each other.
How do I get here from KLIA2? Take the bus to Pudu Sentral and walk, or take the bus to KL Sentral and ride the LRT one stop to Pasar Seni (klia2.info).
Where Petaling Street is

Petaling Street, or Jalan Petaling, runs between Jalan Hang Lekir and Jalan Sultan, opposite the Kotaraya shopping complex and a short walk from Central Market (klia2.info). In Chinese it is 茨厂街. The nearest train is Pasar Seni on the LRT Kelana Jaya Line (Tourism Malaysia), the next station from KL Sentral on the same line (klia2.info).

The street had a makeover recently. Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) replaced the roof, rewired the street and rearranged the hawker spaces into covered, more orderly rows, with completion expected by 1 May 2026 (The Malaysian Reserve). Expect newer stall layouts than older photos show. Save Pasar Seni station in your map app before you fly.
Breakfast and kopitiam on Jalan Balai Polis and Jalan Hang Lekir

Mornings start early here. Tourism Malaysia notes the wet market is busy in the early hours, with fruit, vegetables and seafood on sale (Tourism Malaysia). That is when the breakfast shops do their trade.
Ho Kow Hainam Kopitiam is at 1 Jalan Balai Polis. Google Maps lists it as a breakfast and brunch restaurant, cafe and coffee shop. Order a kopi and some toast and watch the street wake up.

On the same row, at 3 Jalan Balai Polis, is Bunn Choon. It describes itself as a heritage Chinese restaurant and pastry shop serving egg tarts, traditional Chinese pastries and Hong Kong-style dim sum since 1893, beside Kwai Chai Hong (Bunn Choon). Its menu also lists dumplings, radish cake, soups and desserts.

For something hot and savoury, Hon Kee Porridge is at 93 Jalan Hang Lekir. Pelago recommends its raw fish porridge, made with sliced snakehead fish, with white pepper on top (Pelago). Tourism Malaysia lists Hon Kee as non-halal (Tourism Malaysia). Go before mid-morning and walk to Kwai Chai Hong afterwards for the murals.
Noodles: Hokkien mee, lala, beef and asam laksa

Restaurant Kim Lian Kee is at 49 Jalan Petaling. Pelago describes its Hokkien mee as noodles fried in a thick soy sauce gravy with prawns, pork, cabbage and lard fritters, and also recommends its chee cheong fun, rice noodle rolls in sweet bean and chilli sauce (Pelago). This is a pork dish.

Kedai Kopi Lai Foong is at 138 Jalan Tun H S Lee. Pelago describes its lala noodles as rice noodles in a clam broth with Chinese wine and ginger (Pelago). Tourism Malaysia lists Lai Foong lala noodles as non-halal (Tourism Malaysia).

On Jalan Sultan, Kim Yong Gee Beef Noodle at number 22 is listed on Google Maps as a Chinese noodle restaurant. At 95 Jalan Hang Lekir, Koon Kee Wan Tan Mee is listed as a hawker stall and Chinese takeaway for wantan mee.

Looking for asam laksa on Petaling Street? Asam Laksa Petaling Street is at 63 Jalan Petaling, listed on Google Maps as a Chinese noodle restaurant and a Malay restaurant. Asam laksa is a sour, fish-based noodle soup, so ask about the broth if you have allergies.

Mee Tarik Restoran is on Jalan Sultan, at number 36. Its kitchen is built around house-made, hand-pulled noodles, from a spicy curry noodle bowl to a classic noodle soup, and its listing says it often stays open until 6am.
Landing late? Mee Tarik is one answer. The supper in Kuala Lumpur guide has more.
Hawker stalls and the food court

Tourism Malaysia names Tang City Food Court at 21-27 Jalan Hang Lekir as one of the hawker spots to check, and lists it as non-halal (Tourism Malaysia). A food court lets a group order from several stalls and sit together. Pelago also points to a fried sweet potato ball cart outside it (Pelago).

Along the street itself, Pelago lists stalls for tau foo fah and soya bean milk, muah chee rolled in peanuts, and apam balik peanut pancakes on Jalan Hang Lekir (Pelago). Stall positions changed in the upgrade, so walk the street once and stop at whatever is cooking.

For Nyonya food, Peranakan Place has a branch on Jalan Petaling. The group describes its cooking as Nyonya cuisine that blends Malay and Chinese flavours (Peranakan Place). Ask about halal status at the counter.
Bring small notes in case a stall does not take cards, then pick one dish from each of two or three stalls instead of one big meal.
Sit-down dinner and drinks
When the evening market starts, the shophouses along Jalan Petaling turn into dinner spots and bars.

Da Bao Restobar at 145 Jalan Petaling is listed on Google Maps as a gastropub and cocktail bar, and Tourism Malaysia lists it as non-halal (Tourism Malaysia). Chocha Foodstore at 156 Jalan Petaling is described on Google Maps as a calm garden cafe with a modern menu of Asian-influenced flavours, and it also lists itself as a cocktail and wine bar.

Junk Cafe at 124 Jalan Petaling is an antique-filled bar and bistro. Its website says the menu is pork-free, it opens daily at 11am, and a live band plays on Friday and Saturday from 9.15pm (Junk Cafe). Pork-free is not the same as halal certified.
For plant-based food, The Hungry Tapir is at 135 Jalan Petaling. It serves East-meets-West sharing plates made from plants, with a full-service bar, and it takes larger groups and dogs.
The vegan restaurant guide for Kuala Lumpur lists more plant-based kitchens. Book a table for the weekend if you are a group.
Halal food on a mixed street

Petaling Street is a mix. Tourism Malaysia says both halal and non-halal options are available around the area, and marks several of the Chinese stalls and restaurants named here as non-halal (Tourism Malaysia). A Google Maps label or the word "halal" in a name is the business's own description. A shop that says pork-free may still serve alcohol or use non-certified suppliers. If halal matters to you, look for the JAKIM halal certificate on the wall before you order.
Getting to Petaling Street from KLIA2

The bus from KLIA2 to Pudu Sentral leaves from the KLIA2 Transportation Hub on Level 1, and ttklia.com lists the route as KL City Centre (Pudu Sentral) (ttklia.com). From the Pudu Sentral area, Petaling Street is a short walk (klia2.info). The fare is shown on the booking page. See the KLIA2 bus station guide for finding the hub.

Staying near KL Sentral? Take the bus there, then the LRT Kelana Jaya Line one stop to Pasar Seni, the station Tourism Malaysia names as closest to Petaling Street (klia2.info), (Tourism Malaysia). The first night in KL guide matches each bus stop to dinner nearby.

Frequently Asked Questions
What is Petaling Street food known for?
Petaling Street food is known for Chinese hawker dishes and dim sum (Tourism Malaysia). Look for Hokkien mee, chee cheong fun, lala noodles, beef noodles, raw fish porridge and egg tarts.
What to eat in Petaling Street for breakfast?

For Petaling Street breakfast, try raw fish porridge at Hon Kee on Jalan Hang Lekir, egg tarts and dim sum at Bunn Choon on Jalan Balai Polis, or kopi and toast at Ho Kow Hainam Kopitiam on the same street.
Is Petaling Street food halal?
Not all of it. Petaling Street has halal and non-halal places side by side, and many Chinese stalls serve pork. Check for the JAKIM halal certificate at each counter.
Where can I find asam laksa on Petaling Street?
Asam Laksa Petaling Street is at 63 Jalan Petaling. Open its Google Maps listing for directions and hours.
What time does Petaling Street open?
Tourism Malaysia lists Petaling Street as open 8am to 8pm Sunday to Friday and 8am to 10pm on Saturday (Tourism Malaysia). Breakfast stalls open earlier, and each shop sets its own hours.
How do I get to Petaling Street from KL Sentral?
Take the LRT Kelana Jaya Line from KL Sentral one stop to Pasar Seni, then walk to Petaling Street (klia2.info).
Conclusion

Petaling Street food runs from porridge and egg tarts at breakfast to Hokkien mee, lala noodles and asam laksa at lunch, then gastropubs and plant-based plates in the evening. Mix and match stalls, ask about halal at each one, and keep small notes. The places above come from Google Maps listings on 5 November 2026, so open each Maps link to check opening hours before you go.
Ready to plan the trip in? Book the bus from KLIA2 to Pudu Sentral on ttklia.com and walk to Chinatown for your first meal.
